VelocityBench — machine-readable guide
======================================

WHAT THIS IS
  One benchmark sweep rendered as a single self-contained page. Exactly ONE
  run on ONE hardware target. No cross-run or cross-hardware mixing, ever — the
  generator refuses two JSON files.

RUN IDENTITY
  timestamp:            2026-07-25T11:50:24+00:00
  target_host:          10.7.0.2
  cpu_model:            AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor
  postgres_version:     17.10 (Debian 17.10-1.pgdg13+1)
  load_generator:       k6-v2.0.0
  concurrency:          40
  duration_secs:        30
  tview_mode:           logged
  tview_trigger_scope:  fraiseql-only
  fraiseql_version:     2.14.0

DATA
  Machine copy of this run + metadata:  ./data.json
    { "run": <raw run JSON>, "scenarios": <the scenarios.json contract> }
  Committed source run JSON (provenance):  bench-hetzner-2026-07-25-median.json

RESULT-ROW GLOSSARY  (run.results[])
  framework   engine under test (see FRAMEWORKS below)
  query       THE SCENARIO ID — the field is named "query", NOT "scenario"
  rps         requests/second (for MC1: cycles/second, a workflow metric)
  p50_ms / p95_ms / p99_ms   latency percentiles, milliseconds
  requests    total requests issued in the measured window
  errors      failed/non-2xx responses; 0 on every published cell
  rss_steady_mb / rss_max_mb   resident memory
  cold_start_ms   time to first served request

THE GRID — three cell states, no silent gaps
  RESULT              one row in results[]; carries rps + latency + errors.
  EXCLUDED BY DESIGN  the (framework, scenario) pair is structurally N/A. It is
                      ABSENT from results[] and listed in scenarios.exclusions
                      with a reason_id into scenarios.exclusion_reasons.
                      Excluded is NOT slow and NOT missing by accident.
  NOT MEASURED IN THIS RUN
                      wired in the benchmark but not executed in this sweep;
                      absent from results[] AND absent from exclusions.
                      Distinct from excluded-by-design; neither slow nor
                      excluded on purpose. This publishable run measured the
                      full grid, so no cell carries this status.

CITING A CELL
  Every (framework, scenario) cell has a stable anchor:
    #cell-<framework>-<scenario>      e.g.  #cell-fraiseql-tv-Q1
  Each DOM cell carries data-framework and data-scenario, plus:
    result       data-rps, data-p99-ms, data-errors
    excluded     data-excluded="true", data-reason-id="<N>"
    not measured data-not-measured="true"

M1 — READ THE MECHANISM, NOT JUST THE NUMBER
  M1   FraiseQL's real write: an integrated, column-aware cascade that recomputes
       the affected precomputed rows (logged tview maintenance) so reads stay
       consistent — the slowest write measured here, and the price of
       always-consistent precomputed reads.
       Classical: a vanilla single UPDATE with no derived state.
  FraiseQL losing on the integrated M1 write is a real, prominent result, not an
  artifact — the write-heavy workload shape names a resolver engine, not FraiseQL.
  MC1 is a workflow benchmark, not raw server speed: it counts the client round-trips needed to reach a consistent state after a write. FraiseQL = 1 request/cycle (the mutation response carries the cascade); classical GraphQL and REST = 2 requests/cycle (mutation + serial re-fetch).

REQUEST ANATOMY — QUERY STRATEGIES (S0)
  Where a nested read's round-trips come from, by architecture. Round-trip
  counts are STRUCTURAL truth (provenanced to the source files below), not
  measured timings: resolver + DataLoader adds one BATCHED SQL trip per nesting
  level (Q1/Q2b/Q3 = 1/2/3, WHERE key = ANY($1), so no N+1); compile-to-SQL and
  precompute stay at one round-trip at any depth. The animation's dot pacing is
  the ONLY measured overlay (each engine's p50 for the read).
  DataLoader credit: The classical GraphQL engines here are best-practice, not strawmen: every one batches its nested lookups with a DataLoader (WHERE key = ANY($1)), so there is no N+1 swarm. What the nesting cliff measures is the residual cost — the serial per-level round-trips plus in-process resolver execution — which is exactly what compile-to-SQL and precompute avoid.
  Per-level batched resolvers [resolver-dataloader]
      members: async-graphql, mercurius, apollo-server, strawberry
      SQL round-trips: Q1=1 Q2b=2 Q3=3
      source: frameworks/async-graphql/src/dataloaders.rs
      One HTTP hop, then the root SQL, then one BATCHED SQL per nesting level — each DataLoader coalesces a level's lookups into a single WHERE key = ANY($1) query, so there is no N+1. The residual cost is that those trips are serial (each level waits on the parent's ids) plus in-process resolver execution, so depth adds round-trips.
  Compile the whole query to one SQL [compile-to-sql]
      members: hasura, postgraphile, fraiseql-v-nocache, fraiseql-v-cache
      SQL round-trips: Q1=1 Q2b=1 Q3=1
      source: frameworks/postgraphile/src/index.ts
      The engine compiles the entire GraphQL tree into ONE composed SQL statement (LATERAL joins / jsonb aggregation) and issues a single round-trip that returns the whole nested document — at any depth. Hasura, PostGraphile and FraiseQL's on-the-fly v views are all in this class; FraiseQL·v is one compiler among several, not a category of its own.
  Read a pre-computed JSONB row [precompute]
      members: fraiseql-tv, fraiseql-tv-cache
      SQL round-trips: Q1=1 Q2b=1 Q3=1
      source: frameworks/fraiseql/schema_tv.py
      The nested document is denormalised into a tv_* table at write time, so a read is a single SELECT of pre-built JSONB with no joins — one round-trip at any depth. On a result-cache hit (tv+cache) the database is not touched at all: the path stops at the server.
  Hand-written REST + SQL [rest]
      members: actix-web-rest
      SQL round-trips: Q1=1 Q2b=1 Q3=—
      source: frameworks/actix-web-rest/src/repositories.rs
      No GraphQL document on the wire: each endpoint runs a hand-written SQL (a JOIN for the nested case) — one round-trip like a compiler, but bespoke per endpoint. Not one of the three animated GraphQL lanes; shown here for completeness.
  APQ: APQ (automatic persisted queries) elides the document-upload work of the first hop: instead of sending the whole GraphQL query text, the client sends a 32-byte SHA-256 hash the server has already parsed. It shortens the request hop but changes no SQL round-trip; measured in the Q1_APQ / Q2b_APQ / M1_APQ cells.

MECHANISM LADDER (S2) — where FraiseQL's read speed comes from   (#s2-mechanism-ladder)
  Four FraiseQL variants, the same read, one mechanism added per rung: JOIN
  views (v-nocache) -> + result cache (v-cache) -> tv precompute (tv) -> + result
  cache (tv-cache) -> + APQ (persisted hash). The result cache and APQ change no
  SQL; the tv precompute step is the read win, and it grows with nesting depth.
  Absolute RPS per rung; the delta is over the result rung below it.
  Ladder @ Q2b (rung: RPS, delta over the rung below):
    fraiseql-v-nocache         JOIN views      5,375 RPS
    fraiseql-v-cache           + result cache  5,351 RPS  (−0.4%)
    fraiseql-tv                tv precompute   9,119 RPS  (+70.4%)
    fraiseql-tv-cache          + result cache  9,063 RPS  (−0.6%)
    +APQ (fraiseql-tv-cache)   + APQ           8,739 RPS  (−3.6%)
  precompute step (tv rung over the rung below) by depth: Q1 +10.1%, Q2 +52.4%, Q2b +70.4%, Q3 +110.5%, T1 +71.4%

APQ ISOLATED (S3) — persisted-query hash, before vs after   (#s3-apq)
  Each query/mutation sent as a pre-registered SHA-256 hash instead of full
  text. It changes no SQL round-trip, so any effect is transport-only. Status is
  read from the grid, never a hand-kept capability list: a measured _APQ twin ->
  a real (often ~zero or negative) delta; no twin -> APQ-capable-but-not-measured
  in this run (NOT excluded); by-design N/A -> its verbatim exclusion reason.
   Q1 -> Q1_APQ   measured twins: fraiseql-tv −4.5%, fraiseql-tv-cache −6.5%, fraiseql-v-nocache −5.0%, fraiseql-v-cache −5.9%, async-graphql −0.3%, mercurius −0.4%, apollo-server +0.4%
  Q2b -> Q2b_APQ  measured twins: fraiseql-tv −3.2%, fraiseql-tv-cache −3.6%, fraiseql-v-nocache −4.0%, fraiseql-v-cache −2.5%, async-graphql +3.5%, mercurius −0.4%, apollo-server +4.2%
   M1 -> M1_APQ   measured twins: fraiseql-tv −2.2%, fraiseql-tv-cache +1.9%, fraiseql-v-nocache +0.5%, fraiseql-v-cache +1.3%, async-graphql +6.3%, mercurius −3.4%, apollo-server +2.3%
  excluded by design: hasura [4], postgraphile [5], actix-web-rest [6], strawberry [7]

CACHE UNDER FIRE (S4) — hot pool (HC3) vs rotating keys (C3)   (#s4-cache-under-fire)
  The same single-row lookup two ways: 20 rotating keys (C3, a cache can never
  hit) and a 5-key hot pool (HC3, a cache should hit almost every time). If the
  result cache earned its keep, the cache-on rows would jump C3->HC3 while the
  cache-off rows stayed flat. Delta is HC3 (hit) over C3 (miss); ~zero or
  negative renders as-is.
  C3 (miss) -> HC3 (hit), delta = hit over miss:
    fraiseql-v-nocache   (cache off)  C3 11,184  HC3 11,249  (+0.6%)
    fraiseql-v-cache     (cache on)   C3 11,118  HC3 11,154  (+0.3%)
    fraiseql-tv          (cache off)  C3 11,467  HC3 11,472  (±0.0%)
    fraiseql-tv-cache    (cache on)   C3 11,604  HC3 11,606  (±0.0%)

FRAMEWORKS (12)
  fraiseql-tv          FraiseQL · tv — precomputed tv_* tables, no result cache (family: fraiseql)
  fraiseql-tv-cache    FraiseQL · tv+cache — precomputed tv_* tables + result cache (family: fraiseql)
  fraiseql-v-nocache   FraiseQL · v — on-the-fly JSONB JOIN views, no result cache (family: fraiseql)
  fraiseql-v-cache     FraiseQL · v+cache — on-the-fly JSONB JOIN views + result cache (family: fraiseql)
  fraiseql-tv-audit    FraiseQL · tv+audit — M1-only audit-overhead appendix row (family: fraiseql) [appendix: M1 only]
  hasura               Hasura CE v2 — compiles GraphQL to a single SQL query (family: classical)
  postgraphile         PostGraphile v5 — compiles GraphQL to a single SQL query (family: classical)
  actix-web-rest       Actix (REST) — hand-written REST handlers over SQL (family: classical)
  async-graphql        async-graphql — Rust per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching (family: classical)
  mercurius            Mercurius — Fastify per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching (family: classical)
  apollo-server        Apollo Server — Node per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching (family: classical)
  strawberry           Strawberry — Python per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching (family: classical)

SCENARIOS (15)
  Q1         Flat user list (20 rows) [read, RPS]
  Q2         Flat post list (10 rows) [read, RPS]
  Q2b        Posts + author (1-level nest) [read, RPS]
  Q3         Comments + author + post (2-level nest) [read, RPS]
  F1         Published filter (10 rows) [read, RPS]
  F2         Published filter + author (10 rows) [read, RPS]
  F3         ORDER BY baseline (20 rows) [read, RPS]
  T1         Full blog page (multi-root) [read, RPS]
  C3         Single-row lookup, 20 rotating UUIDs (cache-miss) [read, RPS]
  HC3        Single-row lookup, 5-UUID hot pool (cache-hit) [read, RPS]
  M1         Update user bio (integrated cascade write) [write, RPS]
  MC1        Mutation → consistent state (workflow) [workflow, cycles/s]
  Q1_APQ     Q1 with APQ (persisted query) [read, RPS]
  Q2b_APQ    Q2b with APQ (persisted query) [read, RPS]
  M1_APQ     M1 with APQ (persisted query) [write, RPS]

WORKLOAD SHAPES → WHICH CELLS ANSWER THEM (winner scored on the S7 model)
  Read-heavy → Q1, Q2, Q2b, Q3, T1
      For read-heavy work the precomputed (tv) path wins: it tops the field at Q1, and its edge over FraiseQL's own JOIN-view (v) variants widens with nesting depth — level at Q1, decisive by Q3 — because precompute carries no N+1. Q1 is a strength here, not a soft spot; the cost of the precomputed document is paid on writes, not reads.
      winner @ ~1000:1 reads:writes → precompute (tv_*) (FraiseQL · tv), ~9,054 req/s
  Deeply nested → Q2b, Q3, T1
      The deeper the nesting, the wider FraiseQL's lead — no N+1 by construction. The cost of that read advantage is paid on writes, not reads (see the write trade).
      winner @ ~100:1 reads:writes → precompute (tv_*) (FraiseQL · tv), ~6,881 req/s
  Write-heavy → M1, MC1
      FraiseQL's integrated cascade write (M1) is the price of always-consistent precomputed reads — the slowest write here, and where a write-heavy mix costs it. MC1 reaches a consistent state in one round-trip where classical needs two.
      winner @ ~1:1 reads:writes → resolver + DataLoader (async-graphql), ~7,407 req/s
  Hot-key lookups → C3, HC3
      A hot 5-key pool (HC3) is where a result cache should shine; the 20-UUID miss regime (C3) shows what a cache does when it cannot help. In this run both regimes land flat — the single-row read is already too cheap for the cache to matter.
      winner @ ~1000:1 reads:writes → precompute (tv_*) (FraiseQL · tv), ~9,696 req/s

FOOTPRINT & COST (S6) — RAM, derived €/1M, the storage trade   (#s6-footprint)
  Steady-state process memory and image size are MEASURED; the € figures are
  DERIVED from measured Q1 throughput and the dated price file, not a separate
  measurement:  € / 1M req = price_month / (Q1 RPS × 2,628,000 s) × 10⁶.
  Ranked honestly — hand-written REST is lighter than FraiseQL and shown so. A
  sub-line is omitted (never faked) when this run did not capture that measure.
  steady-state RAM (lightest first): actix-web-rest 5 MB, fraiseql-v-nocache 12 MB, async-graphql 12 MB, fraiseql-tv 12 MB, fraiseql-v-cache 12 MB, fraiseql-tv-cache 12 MB, mercurius 55 MB, apollo-server 65 MB, postgraphile 127 MB, hasura 135 MB, strawberry 187 MB
  €/1M req @ Q1 on ccx33 (derived): fraiseql-tv €0.0054, fraiseql-tv-cache €0.0054, fraiseql-v-cache €0.0059, fraiseql-v-nocache €0.0060, postgraphile €0.0167, actix-web-rest €0.0318, apollo-server €0.0336, hasura €0.0342, mercurius €0.0361, async-graphql €0.0376, strawberry €0.0540
  storage trade (precompute costs disk): tv_comment 2.8× tb_comment, tv_post 2.0× tb_post, tv_user 1.8× tb_user

AMORTIZATION MODEL (S7) — total load vs the read:write ratio
  A DERIVED model, not a measured cell. Sustainable total requests/second for a
  workload of 1 write + r reads = (r+1) / (r/read_rps + 1/write_rps), from
  measured throughput (endpoints: the measured write rps at r->0, read rps at
  r->infinity). FraiseQL moves read cost to write time (the logged cascade), so
  it needs enough reads per write to amortize the write. The cost layer decides
  the winner; SQL round-trip COUNT is structural context, never cost. A derived
  model on the median-of-three inputs; the read:write ratio is your assumption.
  Break-evens at the default read/write (read Q2b, integrated write mode):
  FraiseQL · tv overtakes PostGraphile v5 at ~2 reads/write
  FraiseQL · tv overtakes async-graphql at ~15 reads/write
  FraiseQL · tv overtakes Actix (REST) at ~7 reads/write
